title: Classification and cladistics; Evolution and speciation; Conservation of biodiversity

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Genetic diversity
items.clue: The variety of alleles within a species or population.

items.label: Extinction
items.clue: The disappearance of a species when its last member dies.

items.label: Common ancestor
items.clue: A species from which two or more later species are descended.

items.label: Biodiversity
items.clue: The variety of life in all its forms, levels and combinations.

questions.stem: Which of these changes would a biologist regard as evolution?

options.text: The frequency of an allele for dark wing colour rises in a moth population over many generations.
The muscles a weightlifter enlarges by training are inherited by the weightlifter's children.
An individual Arctic fox grows a thicker and whiter coat each year as winter approaches.
Young chimpanzees learn from adults how to crack nuts with stones, and the skill spreads.

questions.stem: For one gene, two species have identical amino acid sequences in the protein, yet the base sequences of the gene differ at six positions. Which statement explains this?

options.text: They are not evidence of divergence, because they have had no effect on the protein.
The genes must actually be identical, so the six differences are sequencing errors.
Similar environments keep the proteins alike while the DNA of each species drifts apart.
Some base substitutions leave the amino acid that is coded for unchanged.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of speciation?

options.text: A species changes gradually over millions of years until it looks quite different from its ancestors.
A river splits a population into two halves, which are at once regarded as separate species.
An individual is born with a mutation that makes it different from all others of its species.
A population splits into two groups that then become unable to interbreed with each other.

questions.explanation: Speciation is the splitting of a pre-existing species into two or more species that can no longer interbreed. It is the only way in which new species have appeared.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Caribbean monk seal (Neomonachus tropicalis) case study is correct?

options.text: It became extinct only after industrial fishing fleets reached the Caribbean in the twentieth century
It was hunted for the oil in its blubber from the 1490s, an anthropogenic extinction of a marine mammal species
It shows that marine species are otherwise safe, since the open ocean is too large for people to affect them
Its extinction counts as anthropogenic only because seals were killed; the fishing of its prey was a natural pressure

questions.stem: Why do surveys of biodiversity need to be repeated to provide evidence for a biodiversity crisis?

options.text: Repeating a survey is needed only when the first survey was carried out by citizen scientists rather than experts
Repeating a survey finds additional species, and so gives a higher measure of the habitat's biodiversity
A change in species richness or evenness can only be shown by comparing surveys made at two different times
A single thorough survey is sufficient, provided that it covers a wide enough range of habitats around the world

questions.stem: Which factor is the overarching cause of the current biodiversity crisis, driving each of the specific causes?

options.text: Spread of cities over natural habitat
Natural spread of invasive species
Natural climate shifts as in past eras
Growth of the human population

questions.explanation: The guide names human population growth as the overarching cause, with hunting and over-exploitation, urbanization, deforestation and clearance for agriculture, pollution and the spread of pests, diseases and invasive alien species as the specific causes it drives.

questions.stem: Which description of an approach to the conservation of biodiversity is correct?

options.text: Nature reserves conserve species by keeping people out, so no management is needed
Ex situ conservation in zoos can, by itself, secure the future of an endangered animal species
Rewilding restores natural processes to an area, often by reintroducing missing species
Seed banks can store the germ plasm of every plant species by drying and freezing its seeds

questions.stem: Cladistics classifies organisms into unranked clades. Why is the change from the traditional ranked hierarchy to cladistics described as a paradigm shift?

options.text: It draws the same ranked hierarchy of kingdom, phylum and class in a new, tree-shaped form.
It replaces hypotheses with facts, because cladograms are built from DNA sequence data.
It replaces the assumption of fixed ranks with a different framework of nested clades.
It provides a way of measuring the true rank of every group of organisms.

questions.stem: A newly discovered plant species is placed, on the basis of DNA base sequences, in a clade in which every known member produces a particular alkaloid. What can be concluded about the new species?

options.text: It will resemble the other members in appearance, because that is how the clade was defined.
Nothing can be predicted until its morphology has been compared with that of the others.
Only its DNA sequence is known to match the others; no other trait can be inferred.
It is likely to produce the alkaloid, a trait shared by descent within the clade.

questions.stem: What does a node on a cladogram represent?

options.text: A named living or fossil species from which the later lineages are descended.
The point at which one lineage became more advanced than the other lineage.
The hypothetical common ancestor of the lineages that branch from it.
The taxonomic rank, such as family, shared by lineages beyond it.

questions.explanation: A node represents a hypothetical common ancestor: the point at which the lineages arising from it diverged. All the organisms on the branches beyond a node form a clade.

questions.stem: Which evidence was used in 1977 to propose that all organisms should be classified into three domains?

options.text: Visible differences in cell structure seen using the electron microscope.
Comparison of the base sequences of ribosomal RNA across many different organisms.
Evidence that archaea are a subgroup of bacteria, so that all prokaryotes form one domain.
Overall similarity in the appearance and way of life of the organisms being classified.

questions.explanation: The classification of all organisms into three domains was proposed in 1977 using evidence from rRNA base sequences, which showed that prokaryotes fall into two groups as different from each other as either is from eukaryotes.

questions.stem: What do allopatric speciation and sympatric speciation have in common?

options.text: Both require reproductive isolation of the populations, so that their gene pools can diverge.
Both require a physical barrier, though in sympatric speciation the barrier is very small.
Both require the populations to live in separate areas at some stage in the process.
Both are complete as soon as the populations stop interbreeding, before any genetic change.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of a classification in which every group corresponds to evolutionary relationships?

options.text: The groups show which of the organisms are the most advanced.
Every species is given a unique name made up of two parts.
Organisms that look alike are placed together for identification.
Characteristics of members of a group can be predicted.

questions.explanation: When all the members of a taxonomic group have evolved from a common ancestor, characteristics of organisms within the group can be predicted because they are shared within the clade.
